E061-01.notes: Two independent clauses (McCoy was born... / he traveled...). D splits them with a period, and 'As a teenager' introduces the second. A is a comma splice, and 'as a teenager' is also ambiguous between the clauses. B is a fused sentence. C ('Kentucky, as a teenager, and he traveled') attaches 'as a teenager' to the parents' escape and is awkward; the joining is garbled. Facts check out: born 1844 in Ontario to parents who escaped Kentucky, trained in Scotland as a teen.

E061-02.notes: Parallel participles 'shoveling... and oiling' form a modifier of the job. B ('shoveling... and to oil') and D ('shoveled... and oiling') are not parallel. C ('Railroad, he shoveled...') is a comma splice.

E061-03.notes: 'At the time' and 'could oil' put this in the past, and 'every train' is singular, so 'had' is right. A ('every train have') breaks subject-verb agreement. C ('has') is in the present tense and doesn't fit the past context. D ('having') leaves the sentence without a main verb, so it is a fragment.

E061-04.notes: Redundancy. 'steadily' alone carries the meaning. A stacks three synonyms. B ('steadily and continuously') is still redundant. D ('continuously at a constant rate') is wordier and partly redundant. ACT's 'most concise' convention makes C the clear choice.

E061-05.notes: Engines no longer stopping is the cause of the savings, so causal 'since' fits. 'although' and 'whereas' signal a contrast, and 'unless' sets a condition; all three are illogical here.

E061-06.notes: This needs the singular possessive of one man: 'McCoy's lubricator'. A ('McCoys'') is a plural possessive. B ('McCoys') is a plural with no possessive. C ('McCoy lubricator') has no possessive and reads oddly, though it might pass as a noun modifier. D is clearly best.

E061-07.notes: Sentence 7 ends by saying the phrase's origin is disputed. 'Whatever its origin,' sets that aside and moves on to the lasting impact. The other choices fail: the sentence isn't an example of the disputed origin (A), the dispute doesn't cause anything (B), and nothing makes it similar (D).

E061-08.notes: The subject 'McCoy's inventions' and the verb 'kept' should have no punctuation between them. A puts a comma between subject and verb. C turns the verb into a relative clause, so the sentence has no main verb and is a fragment. D puts a semicolon before a clause that has no subject.

E061-09.notes: The passage is a past-tense narrative, so 'went on to receive' fits. B (present), C (future) and D (present progressive) all shift tense for no reason.

E061-10.notes: The essay is a short biography that mentions the phrase in only one sentence and calls its origin disputed. A says the essay 'proves' the origin, which contradicts it. C gives an irrelevant reason. D is false, because sentence 7 mentions the phrase.

E061-11.notes: This needs the singular possessive 'work's importance'. A ('works') has no apostrophe. C ('work is importance') inserts a verb and makes no sense. D ('work importance') has no possessive. Note: this item comes from a different passage (CLD-P-ACT-E-000060) than the rest of the batch. That is not a defect in the item.
